Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares what their own critic says, and the cards stay private. Name where critic lines come from without blaming anyone’s family. Pass “worthless” or “hopeless” to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Show of hands: a few, a quarter, half, almost everyone. Next slide shows the answer. The critic works the same way: it treats every slip as if the whole room saw.

Slide 3 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 4 · Notes

Paul Gilbert’s model; it doesn’t map to brain regions. The critic attacks you before anyone else can; in a strange way, it’s trying to protect you. Private question: whose voice does your critic sound like? Nobody answers out loud.

Slide 5 · Notes

Thumbs up, down or sideways. Next slide shows the answer. Self-compassion means honest about the mistake, kind about the person.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 7 · Notes

“I’m having the thought that I’m an idiot” is a thought; “I’m an idiot” is a verdict. Check the evidence: fact or opinion? Trying to shut the critic up backfires (the white bear). Notice it, then redirect.

Slide 8 · Notes

People who prepped for a stressful speech by talking to themselves by name or as “you” felt less anxious and gave better speeches than people who used “I.”

Two minutes. Nobody shares what their own critic says.

Slide 10 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for honest plus kind.

Slide 11 · Notes

Pairs name the voice: critic, coach, or shrug. “Tests don’t matter” is the shrug; it skips the useful part.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

The spotlight effect again: most people notice less than you think, and forget faster.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

More than one good answer. The best one is the one you’d actually use.

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 17 · Notes

Private; the card goes home. Fact or opinion? Then the coach’s version, using your name, and one specific thing to try next time, if anything. Writing nothing is fine.

Name it without blaming anyone’s family. Some lines start as messages about race, sexuality or body.

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why the inner critic sounds so convincing (it runs on the threat system), what research says about self-compassion and effort, and how to get some distance from the voice. Each student privately rewrites one critic line as a coach on their side would say it.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 2 minThe T-shirt guess
  2. 2 minWhere the critic lives
  3. 2 minDoes being hard on yourself keep you sharp?
  4. 3 minDistance from the voice, and use your name
  5. 3 minCoach lines: turn and talk, share out
  6. 4 minThree moments: Jordan, Ella, Leo
  7. 4 minRewrite your critic, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The T-shirt guess, the quick vote, and the private rewrite.

Before you teach
Keep the critic's lines private.

Nobody reads their card aloud or says what their critic tells them. The cards go home with the student.

Worthless or hopeless goes to a counselor.

If a student says the critic is loud most of the day, or that they feel worthless or hopeless, thank them, don't explore it in the circle, and connect them with a counselor that day. Don't ask screening questions in advisory.

When the critic is about bodies or food.

Keep every example away from weight, shape and eating. If a student's critic is mostly about their body, food or weight, that's a counselor conversation. The student page lists help for that.

Respect where a voice came from.

Some students hear their critic in a parent's, coach's or grandparent's words. Don't invite anyone to criticize their family. The point from the student page is that a voice can be loving at its source and still not get the last word.

The SAT card can land hard.

Juniors and seniors may be in testing season. Keep it on the character, and don't ask anyone about their own scores.

Don't push affirmations.

If a student says "just tell yourself you're amazing," gently note that glowing lines you don't believe can make the gap feel bigger. Aim for fair and kind.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Messages about race and background.

Some critic lines start as messages students absorbed about their race, culture or background. Name that once, plainly, as something that comes from outside. Don't ask anyone to share which messages they've heard.

High expectations at home.

Some families show love through high expectations and blunt feedback, and for many students that's where drive comes from. Present it as loving and still able to leave a harsh voice behind. Avoid "In X families" generalizations, and say "parent or caregiver."

LGBTQ+ students.

The critic can repeat messages about sexuality or gender identity. If a student raises it privately, connect them with a counselor, who can also share The Trevor Project (1-866-488-7386, or text START to 678-678) and, for gender identity, Trans Lifeline (877-565-8860).

Students who've heard a lot of correction.

Students with ADHD, learning differences or a learning plan have often heard more correction than praise, and the critic may sound like years of it. The evidence file helps here. Never use a diagnosis as a casual adjective.

Bodies of every size.

Body talk is part of many students' critic. Keep examples on grades, sports and friendships, and never offer weight loss or appearance as a fix.

Retakes and tutoring cost money.

In the SAT moment, "do I want to retake it?" assumes the fee and time are there. Point out that a coach voice works whether or not a retake happens, and that the college counseling office can talk through options.

What the research says

Psychologist Paul Gilbert describes three emotion systems: threat, drive and soothing. Self-critical people tend to underuse soothing, so the threat system runs unchecked. It's a model of how emotions work and doesn't map to brain regions.

Gilbert, 2009, Advances in Psychiatric Treatment

After failing a hard test, college students prompted to treat themselves with compassion studied longer for a retest than students prompted to boost their self-esteem, or given no prompt.

Breines and Chen, 2012, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

A review of 19 studies with more than 7,000 adolescents found a large link between higher self-compassion and lower anxiety, depression and stress. These are correlations, so they show a strong connection without proving cause.

Marsh, Chan and MacBeth, 2018, Mindfulness

Students who walked into a room in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed. Fewer than a quarter did. Psychologists call it the spotlight effect.

Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky, 2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

People who prepped for a stressful speech by talking to themselves by name or as "you" felt less anxious and gave better speeches than people who used "I."

Kross et al., 2014, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

People told not to think about a white bear ended up thinking about it more.

Wegner et al., 1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
